entries.title: Progressive Peggy Flanagan Wins Minnesota's Democratic Senate Primary
entries.summary: Flanagan's victory over Angie Craig helps cap off a primary cycle for progressives in which they notched several high-profile wins.
entries.content:
Peggy Flanagan is the projected winner in Minnesota’s Senate Democratic primary, a race that tested how much fuel progressive candidates have in statewide contests.

Flanagan, the state’s lieutenant governor, beat Rep. Angie Craig, lining her up to run against Republican Michele Tafoya in the general election. Craig, a centrist who flipped a Republican House seat for Democrats in 2018, ran against Flanagan in a test of moderates versus progressives within the party, a battle that has played out in other primaries.

Flanagan earned the endorsement of several progressives, including Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, and the support of Sen. Tina Smith, whose retirement is leaving the seat up for grabs. The Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, which is the equivalent of a state Democratic party, backed Flanagan over Craig in the contest.

Craig skipped the convention where delegates of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party picked a candidate, saying the endorsement process “does not reflect the full scope of the party.”

Craig, who raised $12.7 million as of July 22, outraised Flanagan, who raised about $6.5 million in the same period.

The state has been a Democratic stronghold for decades, and it’s been the stage for some recent national issues and debates, from the murder of George Floyd in 2020 to the aggressive presence of federal agents during Operation Metro Surge that resulted in the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti earlier this year. 

The administration’s actions in the Twin Cities played a key role in the state’s primaries.

Flanagan criticized Craig for her vote in favor of the Laken Riley Act, named after a college student who was murdered by an undocumented immigrant, which allows federal law enforcement to detain and deport immigrants for certain nonviolent crimes. Craig has since told voters she regretted that vote because of the additional powers it granted federal agents.

Craig losing is also a blow to the party leaders who backed her, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Minnesota first lady Gwen Walz.

Gov. Tim Walz, who has been embroiled in controversy surrounding investigations of fraud in the state, remained quiet in the primary.

Advance Native Political Leadership, a national and Native-led organization that seeks to elect more Native Americans, also backed Flanagan.

Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, would be the first Native American woman to serve in the Senate if elected.
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: Trump Says He Followed Secret Service Guidance to Switch Planes
entries.summary: “I just follow what they like to do,” Trump said of sneaking onto a different plane out of Turkey.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump confirmed he did not travel on Air Force One with White House staff and reporters after a NATO summit in Turkey, but was instead secreted onto a separate plane at the behest of the Secret Service and the military due to a security threat.

“It’s only up to Secret Service,” Trump said. “I just follow what they like to do. So I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, different plane. Equal safety, but they wanted me to do it, so I do it. ”

The Washington Post reported Monday that Trump was not aboard the presidential 747 that serves as Air Force One when it departed the summit on July 8, despite boarding the plane with cameras rolling. After boarding, the president was transferred via a catering truck to a waiting military aircraft.

The aircraft carried Trump to RAF Mildenhall military base in England, while reporters and White House staff flew there on the legacy Air Force One. The president reboarded Air Force One at Mildenhall, leaving reporters and some staff believing he had been aboard the entire trip.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller remained aboard the legacy Air Force One for the flight to Britain.

Prior to leaving, Trump announced the new Qatari-donated jet replacing the old Air Force One aircraft would fly to Mildenhall early so the troops could see the new plane. He said he would follow later on the traditional Air Force One “for old times sake.” The New York Times later reported that the change was made due to a potential threat from Iran and the new jet’s lack of defensive capabilities.

The new Air Force One carried the president and reporters to the summit.

The ruse to conceal the president’s whereabouts from some staff, the press pool and the world was a departure from conventional communication about presidential travel, even in times of crisis. It parallels then-President Bill Clinton’s trip to Pakistan in 2000, when he arrived in an unmarked aircraft after the plane he was thought to be in had already landed.

However, some members of the press were informed about Clinton’s charade.

In Ankara, Turkey, in July, after boarding for the first leg of the return Air Force One flight, reporters were told to keep their window blinds closed, citing instructions from the Secret Service. Video of the departure showed a catering truck parked beside the legacy Air Force One when Trump boarded, then pulling away and driving to a waiting aircraft in the distance.

The bait and switch resulted from the latest reported threat from Iran against the president’s life, amid renewed military strikes between the United States and Iran after a ceasefire agreement collapsed.

After leaving Mildenhall, a reporter asked the president why they had to close the window blinds and if there was a credible threat by Iran against Air Force One.

“I have a threat all the time,” Trump said at the time. “I’m number one on their list, before you. But if I go, you go. Right?”
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Longtime Rep. John Larson Loses Reelection Bid in Connecticut
entries.summary: The 78-year-old faced questions about his age and health in the run-up to Tuesday’s primary election.
entries.content:
Longtime Connecticut Rep. John Larson lost his reelection bid Tuesday in yet another tough Democratic primary fueled by voters’ desire for generational change.

The Associated Press called the race Tuesday night for former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, who received the state’s Democratic endorsement in an upset win at a convention in May. Throughout his campaign, Bronin asserted that the endorsement was part of a “political earthquake” and signaled the Democratic Party’s needed shakeup.

Leading up to the primary, the 78-year-old Larson faced questions about his age and health after suffering a complex partial seizure during a speech on the House floor in February 2025. Larson previously said the medical episode was a side effect from a heart valve replacement he had more than 15 years ago.

Younger, and often more progressive, candidates have claimed a series of victories during the 2026 election cycle.

Larson, who is in his 14th term in Congress, defended his reelection campaign by emphasizing his experience, commitment to adjusting Social Security benefits and his willingness to stand up to President Donald Trump. Larson said in a July 29 debate that his seat “will be open soon enough, but we’re in the middle of a crisis.”

Larson said he was poised to become the chair of the House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security if Democrats regained control of the chamber after November.

“If you’re coming to Congress for the first time, you start at the bottom and work your way up,” Larson said in an interview with a local outlet. “But if you have the opportunity to send someone who’s going to be a chairman, that means your voice in your district is amplified.”

Bronin will face Republican Amy Chai in November.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Darline Graham and Ralph Norman Head to a Runoff in South Carolina
entries.summary: The two Republicans will compete to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham for a full Senate term.
entries.content:
Two Republicans are headed to a runoff for the party’s nomination for Lindsey Graham's old Senate seat, after none of the 10 people running received a majority in Tuesday’s primary.

Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister, and Rep. Ralph Norman advanced to the Republican runoff on Aug. 25.

Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term last month. Most expected her to fill the role on an interim basis, but she expressed interest in running for the full term just a week into her tenure. President Donald Trump, who was personally close to the late senator, endorsed her for the full term.

Little is known about Graham’s political views, even by her Republican colleagues, as she has spent the majority of her life outside the public eye. She has avoided questions in the Capitol and has had limited interaction with local reporters in South Carolina.

Norman, a House member who previously ran unsuccessfully for governor, is known for being a thorn in the side of both House Republican leadership and Trump. He endorsed former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley in the 2024 presidential election and routinely votes against the party’s agenda in Congress.

Despite this, Norman is viewed as a staunch conservative among voters and is a longtime member of the House Freedom Caucus. He is sure to face staunch opposition from Trump’s political orbit in his bid for the Senate seat.

The remaining days will be an all-out sprint for the two candidates as they try to tie themselves as closely to Trump as possible and secure the nomination.

The winner will take on Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.
entries.author: Reese Gorman

entries.title: Inside a D.C. Courtroom Pushed to Its Limit Under Trump
entries.summary: On a Monday in August, the 113 cases reviewed in courtroom C-10 represented a transformed criminal justice system.
entries.content:
Attorney Charles Murdter’s role in D.C. Superior Court is narrow: Get his temporary clients through the day, and, hopefully for them, out of the front door of the courthouse instead of back to a jail cell.

Or, as he tells them in a speech he’s perfected over time: “My job is to get you the hell out of here.”

It’s a speech he has been giving a lot more lately.

Murdter, part of a rotating panel of lawyers appointed to represent people for their initial court appearances, has watched D.C.’s criminal justice system balloon over the past year. A surge of federal law enforcement ordered by President Donald Trump last August, combined with a shift in posture by the city’s Trump-appointed criminal prosecutor, is continuing to flood the courthouse with defendants.

D.C. police stops last year increased by 13% after Trump’s Aug. 11, 2025, order declaring a crime emergency in the District, according to stop data released by D.C. police. The D.C. jail’s population has soared. Crime, which was already falling steeply before Trump intervened, has remained at historic lows, though assaults with dangerous weapons are up compared to last year, according to D.C. police data. And the days in courtroom C-10 have gotten longer; in June, the court started moving the start time for initial appearances up two-and-a-half hours, to 11 a.m., because court staff had been staying past midnight too often to handle the crush of cases.

On no day is that increase felt more than on Mondays, when everyone locked up over the weekend gets brought into courtroom C-10. Before August of last year, a typical Monday saw 60 to 80 lockups, frequent court observers say. But now, that number is routinely over 100. Sometimes 120. Sometimes 130.

"C-10 is a huge time-suck," said Murdter.

The proceedings of Monday, Aug. 3, began with U.S. Marshals marching a parade of shackled men and women from jail cells to C-10, which is located in the basement of D.C. Superior Court. They were there to make their initial appearance before a judge, learn who their lawyer is, and find out whether they would be locked up or set free until their next court hearing.

As is typical of any day in court, the cases offered a snapshot of enduring societal challenges: violence, addiction, mental illness, poverty. A man arrested for acting erratically with a pocket knife outside the McPherson Square Metro station told an attorney that he didn’t have a cellphone, a case worker or any way to call his lawyer after he left the courthouse. Another was arrested on a domestic violence charge, then ordered to stay away from the woman he had married just two days earlier. A young person was released with a warning from the judge: “Don’t hit your mother again.”

But the 113 cases reviewed in court on Monday also elucidated a newer phenomenon: a local criminal justice system transformed by Trump and his appointees.

Federal surge D.C. AP - 25242591757827 (5410x3607, AR: 1.50)
One of Murdter’s first cases of the day involved arrests made by a U.S. Park Police officer assigned to the “Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Again” initiative, which Trump created last year via executive order to boost city policing. The officer was patrolling with special agents from Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that also sits on the local policing task force, when they saw a group of men, including one who was smoking what the officer “suspected to be a marijuana cigarette,” according to charging documents. After the police approached and searched the Mazda next to the group, they found a pistol, a husky knife and some loose rounds. Two of the men in the group said it wasn’t theirs. Another, Murdter’s client, declined to speak with officers. All three were arrested.

That kind of federal presence in local policing has exploded over the past year — a trend that continued in the lockups that day, records show.

Of the 113 cases discussed in court on Aug. 3, arrest records or charging documents were not readily available for 63 (in many instances because they were domestic-violence related and therefore not public, or because prosecutors did not pursue charges). But among the rest, the federal imprint was vast: Federal officers were present for or involved in half of the arrests.

A handful were joint D.C. police-DEA drug busts or U.S. Park Police arrests on or near federal land — typical activity in the capital city, even before Trump’s 2025 order.

Most, however, appeared to be a product of the convoy-style policing that D.C. residents have become accustomed to over the past year. Marked D.C. police cruisers, followed by a parade of marked or unmarked vehicles full of agents from an alphabet soup of federal agencies: the U.S. Marshals Service, the FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, Customs and Border Protection and the Diplomatic Security Service.

A quarter of the charging documents specifically stated that officers were patrolling as part of the “D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force.” Officers with the task force stopped people for driving illegal ATVs, for smoking marijuana in public, for having license plate covers or tinted windows, for having open containers of alcohol, the arrest records show. Often, the initial alleged violation then led to other findings by police: drugs, guns.

One of the biggest factors contributing to the long days in court is the charging posture from U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro’s office, said court spokesman Doug Buchanan. Pirro, appointed by Trump, is responsible for prosecuting most adult crimes in the District.

“The truth of the matter is that federal prosecutors are moving forward with more cases rather than declining them, pushing more workload into an already overloaded system,” Buchanan wrote in an email where he described the courts as “near collapse” and in desperate need of more federal funding.

Pirro’s office did not respond to a request for comment. 

The number of felony cases filed in D.C. Superior Court increased by 44% last year, according to the D.C. Sentencing Commission. Half of those cases were filed between September and December.

“Not all the cases are good cases,” said Murdter, who said that he sees a lot more being dismissed relatively early in the process.

Around midday, a few dozen activists with Free D.C. — the ubiquitous face of resistance to Trump’s interventions in the District — gathered outside the courthouse to protest the surge in arrests and prosecutions.

They chanted: “We want justice, you say how? End the occupation now!”

Someone in a pink blow-up frog suit held a sign that read: “Jeanine Pirro should be disbarred.”

AP25338771833466 (8352x5567, AR: 1.50)
Behind them, in a corner by the courthouse door, was James Stroud, standing with a cart full of supplies for those emerging from the courthouse after nights in jail. He said he’s been volunteering here, offering phone calls, snacks and shoelaces to people emerging from C-10 for the past two years.

“We've had some days we're out till like 1 a.m.,” he said, adding that the change had been “definitely very significant since Trump took over.”

Back inside, in the court basement, the initial hearings continued. In two cases, Murdter requested that his clients be released not from the courthouse, but from the D.C. jail. Asked later, he said that was because they were immigrants and he heard that ICE was hanging around the courthouse.

“I’m not sure how the word gets out, but it filters down,” he said.

Murdter acknowledged that some people might think immigrants who are in the country illegally and are accused of crimes should be deported. But “when I’m in here, I don’t care about the politics of it,” he said. His job is to zealously represent each client’s best interests — and it’s not in his clients’ best interests to be picked up by ICE.

The afternoon turned into evening. Some in the gallery had been sitting there for hours, waiting in the harsh air conditioning for a loved one to be called. A woman crawled inside the sleeves of her T-shirt to stay warm.

One group of friends, among the last to leave the courtroom, learned that prosecutors were declining to pursue marijuana and gun charges against them — at least for now.

“I understand they’re trying to do their job, but they overstep the boundaries,” said one of the men, recounting the way Drug Enforcement Agency officers approached their car the previous day.

The courtroom emptied at close to 8 p.m. An early night, compared to many this summer, the regulars said. “This is my bedtime,” quipped one marshal, who still wasn’t pleased.

Outside the quiet courthouse, a newly unshackled man huddled on a borrowed cellphone while the jail support team packed up. Then Stroud dragged his cart away into the night.

Everyone would be back soon, to do it all again.
entries.author: Jenny Gathright

entries.title: Democrats Are Building Their Opposition to the Protect College Sports Act
entries.summary: Sens. Cory Booker and Chris Murphy hope to spend the next month generating more resistance to the bill.
entries.content:
Late Friday night, in the last hours before the Senate left for August recess, there was still a chance, however slim, that the Protect College Sports Act would go to a vote. Hours earlier, President Donald Trump had posted about the bill on Truth Social, telling senators to stay in Washington until they passed it. Sure, a handful of Republicans had filed last-minute amendments, some of which called for significant changes to the 171-page legislation. But Republicans pushing the bill started riding the president’s endorsement as hard as they could, hoping it would get the PCSA to the floor.

And it was about that time, when there was a “new groundswell of interest in the bill,” as one Senate aide put it, that Sens. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) and Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) went to work. Each called a number of their fellow Democrats to explain why they don’t like the bill. They called labor groups, civil rights groups, all kinds of groups that could strengthen the public and private pushback. Their staffers called one another. A lot.

Around 11:30 p.m., Senate leaders needed unanimous consent to proceed to a vote on the bill. Murphy and Booker objected. Then around 2 a.m., they objected a second time, as did a handful of other lawmakers from both parties, according to multiple aides.

“Booker and Murphy put stakes in the ground and said we’re not moving,” said a lobbyist working on the bill. “And that was basically that.”

According to the bill’s lead sponsors, Majority Leader John Thune agreed to make the bill a priority when the Senate returned in mid-September. But Murphy and Booker hadn’t just compressed the timeline for the bill to pass through the Senate and House before the midterms in November. They also gave themselves five more weeks to build up the Democratic opposition to it.

“This month is now our opportunity to explain what’s in the bill,” Murphy told NOTUS. “And explain to people, and explain to our colleagues on the left, that this is a fundamental civil rights issue. That this is an unprecedented restraint on compensation for student-athletes, but particularly young Black student-athletes.”

Booker and Murphy aren’t new to college sports legislation (or to the sports-politics crossover in general). Booker, a former football player at Stanford, has spent years discussing how — or whether — Congress should regulate college sports. Murphy has, too, while also taking a recent interest in prediction markets and how youth sports have been co-opted by private equity.

But even as Democrats with a genuine interest in sports, their alliance against the PCSA isn’t totally natural. Murphy has occupied the far-left end of discussions on college sports in Congress, previously introducing bills that would have granted athletes employment status and collective bargaining power. Booker, on the other hand, spent a long time negotiating with Republicans like Sens. Ted Cruz of Texas and Jerry Moran of Kansas, who was one of Booker’s co-sponsors on a college sports bill in 2023. Before Cruz partnered with Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) on the PCSA, there were long-running talks between Cruz, Booker and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut). Booker’s main focus has typically been on health and safety protections for athletes.

Where Murphy and Booker align, however — or where they align most — is in believing athletes should have a real say in any college sports legislation, especially if it gives the NCAA an antitrust exemption to regulate compensation and player movement. This is what they stressed to fellow Democrats on Friday, according to a handful of aides. They kept the argument simple. But in the weeks ahead, as Murphy told NOTUS, they plan to drill down on specifics to limit Democratic support.

Murphy has been public with his opposition of the PCSA, at least in spurts. Booker has operated in the background.

The bill has four Democratic co-sponsors in Cantwell and Sens. Chris Coons of Delaware, Peter Welch of Vermont and John Hickenlooper of Colorado. That has long made it seem as if Cruz and Cantwell could secure the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster. But after the SEC and Big Ten agreed to support the bill on July 31, Cruz and Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri), another co-sponsor, set their sights on running the count past 70, if not higher, in hopes of giving the bill momentum heading into the House. And that’s when dissent started coming in from all sides.

The AFL-CIO and its sports council, including most professional players associations, opposed the bill last Wednesday.

The Congressional Black Caucus opposed it the next day, a decision influenced by Booker lobbying the CBC against the bill behind the scenes.

On the other side of the aisle, three Republicans filed an amendment calling for the bill to explicitly protect existing state laws that bar transgender female athletes from competing in women’s sports.

“Booker and Murphy were everywhere at the end of last week,” a Republican Senate aide told NOTUS. “And usually when the opposition to a bill scores a win like this, you only see it get more organized, more emboldened. Cruz and Cantwell have their work cut out.”

“I think there are very few people who understand the implications of this bill,” Murphy said. “It was not ready for prime time on Friday night, and that became apparent to everyone. I don’t think this bill is going to become more popular, and it’s not going to get more popular amongst legislators as time goes on. I give a lot of credit to Maria and Ted, I know how hard they worked on this. But I think it’s going to raise a lot more questions than it’s going to answer about the future of college sports as people get into the details.”

On athlete compensation in particular, the PCSA would permit the NCAA to enforce a quasi salary cap of about $21.3 million per school (for all sports) without legal liability. That cap, established by a massive legal settlement last summer, would keep rising incrementally each academic year. In a revised version of the bill, the lead sponsors also agreed to an annual $22.5 million fund for schools to retain players, which could grow an additional $5 million if money is used to pay athletes in women’s or Olympic sports.

In recent years, big-spending schools have used third-party name, image and likeness (NIL) deals, including through their multimedia rights partners, to spend above the loose cap. One goal of the PCSA is to aggressively regulate — or even eliminate — that kind of over-the-cap spending. Murphy vehemently disagrees with how, in his words, the bill “essentially puts the NCAA and its member schools in charge of determining what endorsement deals athletes can get and what they can't get.” The College Sports Commission would be in charge of enforcing those strengthened compensation rules.

“I just don’t think you can defend caring about the influence and money in college sports only when it pertains to largely Black athletes who are being vastly underpaid in football and basketball,” Murphy said. “This bill doesn’t do anything to constrain endorsement deals for coaches. It doesn't stop billionaires from plowing money into the schools. It only really limits the ability of the highest-value athletes to get paid. And I don’t think that that is going to save college sports.”

And that’s all just a preview of what people will hear when Murphy calls about college sports in the next five weeks.
entries.author: Jesse Dougherty

entries.title: What to Do In the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 14)
entries.summary: Fairs in Maryland and Virginia, fizzy French pop at 9:30 Club and “Peter Pan” at The Publick Playhouse.
entries.content:
Thursday 


Chang-rae Lee talks “A Tender Age”
Politics and Prose, 5015 Connecticut Ave. NW, 7 p.m., free  

Two days after the official publication date for his eighth novel, Korean American novelist Chang-rae Lee comes to Politics and Prose to chat with Kat Chow, a veteran of NPR’s Code Switch. It’s his most autobiographical novel yet, the Pulitzer Prize finalist and PEN Award winner says, and the book is “a classic bildungsroman,” according to The New York Times review. Tracing the challenges of American adolescents who struggle with the dual difficulties of assimilation and absentee immigrant parents makes for a “quietly moving” account of a 10-year-old boy’s violent world.

“Peter Pan” at Bright Star Theatre
Prince George’s Publick Playhouse, 5445 Landover Road, Hyattsville, 10:30 a.m. and noon, $6 to $8

The hottest matinee ticket in town this summer seems to be “Don’t Let The Pigeon Drive the Bus!” at Wolf Trap’s Theatre-in-the-Woods. The Kennedy Center commissioned this popular adaptation of Mo Willems’ picture book in 2019, and clearly DMV parents are glad its back: The entire Wolf Trap sold out weeks ago. As an affordable, available alternative, we suggest grabbing the kids and flying off to Bright Star Theatre’s “Peter Pan.”

More to explore: “Lego Socials” at two D.C. public libraries.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Friday


Montgomery County Agricultural Fair
501 Perry Parkway, Gaithersburg, $18, free for children under 11, 3 pm. to midnight. 

It’s opening day at the DMV’s only farm fair! Scheduled highlights include the goat show, heifer judging, pig races, chainsaw carving demonstrations and the Decorated Toilet & Toilet Seat Contest. All that entertainment is included with the price of admission, but be prepared to pay extra for the Tilt-a-Whirl and other carnival thrills. The 77th annual fair runs through Aug. 22.

Pomplamoose at the 9:30 Club
6815 V St. NW, 8 p.m. doors, $50

The husband-and-wife duo Pomplamoose derives its name from the French word for grapefruit, deliberately spelled wrong. Silly but appropriate nomenclature for a band that specializes in covering spritzy French cafe music and 50 years of Anglophone pop hits. To wit: Their renditions of “Les Champs-Elysses” and “Lovely Day” each have 18 million Spotify streams. Don’t sleep on their medleys either: Somehow the band’s mashup makes “Sweet Dreams” by the Eurythmics and The White Stripes’ sports anthem “Seven Nations Army” go together better than tonic water and Aperol.

More to explore: The 50th annual Arlington County Fair

Saturday 


“American Mosaic” played by the National Symphony Orchestra 
The Filene Center at Wolf Trap, 1551 Trap Road, Vienna, $49 to $121, kids free with purchase of adult tickets, 8 p.m.

With the Kennedy Center (mostly) shuttered and no concerts scheduled (yet) for next season, time may be running out to see the National Symphony Orchestra. Saturday’s performance should be a quality crowd-pleaser, anchored by “American Mosaic," composer Peter Boyer’s suite accompanied by photography from all 50 states. After intermission, Kennedy Center Honors recipient Renee Fleming joins the orchestra onstage to sing selections from the American songbook. The concert also includes symphonic selections from “West Side Story” and “American in Paris.”

“Gruesome Playground Injuries" at Keegan Theatre
1742 Church Street, 8 p.m., $45 to $55

Dupont Circle’s Keegan Theatre holds down an odd niche in the DMV theatre landscape: It’s one of few District theatres that does not employ professional Equity actors. Instead, the company hires the area’s best hobbyists and up-and-comers to stage a mix of new plays, classics and musicals. Keegan’s 30th anniversary season opens with Rajiv Joseph’s “Gruesome Playground Injuries,” a two-person show about childhood friends who reconnect to reflect on the scraped knees of days gone by.

More to explore: Panda Fest Asian food festival on Pennsylvania Avenue.

Sunday 


No Headliners Tour at Songbyrd
540 Penn St. NE, 7 p.m., $19.32

With its Blue Bottle, oyster bars and Warby Parker, Union Market may seem like too bougie a spot to catch an up-and-coming Eritrean American rapper, but never underestimate the idiosyncrasy of Songbyrd Music House. The No Headliners Tour offers a cross-country lineup of rap and R&B artists, including HENO., who recently released a collaboration with Oddisee. Organizers promise “a community-driven atmosphere, centered on authenticity, discovery, and meaningful connection.”

“Unearthed: Mining on Film” at the National Gallery
East Building, 4th and Constitution, NW. 2 p.m., free

It’s August, and the NGA is digging deep with its weekend film series. On Sunday afternoon, the museum screens two documentaries that explore the geographic, economic and social impacts of mineral extraction. Bill Morrison’s “The Miners’ Hymns” debuted in 2011, but includes a century of archival footage shot in Durham, England. “Louisana Story” (1948) was bankrolled by Standard Oil and depicts mid-century oil extraction through the eyes of a young Cajun boy. Both films complement the exhibition “Beneath the Surface: Mining and American Photography.”

More to explore: String quartet tribute to Destiny’s Child at The Howard Theatre, narrated by Beyonce’s dad.
entries.author: Rebecca Ritzel

entries.title: Merkley Unveils Bill to Combat Trump’s ‘Authoritarianism’
entries.summary: The Oregon Democrat released a 10-point plan to curb the powers of President Trump and his successors.
entries.content:
Sen. Jeff Merkley unveiled a sweeping legislative plan to reassert congressional power over the executive branch, building on his marathon 2025 speech which accused President Donald Trump of abusing his office.

“This is a president trying to become a strongman authoritarian,” Merkley, a Democrat from Oregon, said on the latest episode of the On NOTUS podcast. “If we don't repair the Constitution, we don't have a republic.”

Merkley’s 10-point “For Our Republic Act” would insulate inspectors general and nonpartisan civil service from interference without the consent of Congress, ban recissions from congressionally appropriated funds and extend bribery and ethics statutes to the president and vice president.

It would also ban U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from using biometric surveillance technologies and remove immigration judges from the purview of the attorney general.

While the act targets specific actions linked to Trump, Merkley said it is important to prevent future presidents of either party from having the power to undertake similar actions.

“If we don't address them, another president in the future may say, ‘Hey, there is a pattern for a strongman and I want to do what I want to do, regardless of the laws,’” Merkley said. “We’ve got to say no, that path is no longer available.”

Merkley said he does not expect to pick up any Republican support in this Congress but would support reforming the filibuster to ease its passage.

“We should use every power, including, I would argue, a talking filibuster reform here in the Senate, to be able to have a big debate in front of the public, but eventually get to the possibility of passing laws, even if there is extensive Republican obstruction,” Merkley said.

Weighing in on the debate inside his party playing out in recent political contests, Merkley said Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan was a “good result,” and praised El-Sayed’s economic messaging.

“Understand the reason he caught fire is he said, ‘Look, billionaires are running this country,’” Merkley said. “He's going to take it to the people of Michigan and they're going to decide who's going to represent them. And I sure as hell hope they choose someone to represent them that is willing to fight for families instead of being a pawn for corporations.”

With a growing number of socialists expected to join the House Democratic Caucus after the midterms, Merkley said the moniker is a “charged term” that is divorced from actual policy, and that labels often do more harm than good.

“I don't know that there is a difference, and that's why the labels are so dangerous,” Merkley said. “I was asked in a debate, ‘Are you calling yourself a progressive?’ I said, ‘Call me anything you want. Here's what I stand for.’”

Merkley is set to become the chair of the Senate Budget Committee if Democrats win a majority in November, and said his priority would be controlling debt caused by the Trump administration.

“We are running a 6% of GDP structural deficit that is creating a vortex of debt that will undermine our ability to invest in families and infrastructure,” Merkley said.



On NOTUS is a weekly podcast where NOTUS reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here.
entries.author: Ed Demaria, Igor Bobic

entries.title: No ID, No Money, No Way Out: DHS Deports a Man to a Country He Doesn't Know
entries.summary: The Trump administration sent Rogelio Bolufé, a Cuban national, to a cartel city in Ecuador with no means of escape.
entries.content:
Guayaquil, ECUADOR — Rogelio Bolufé stared out the porthole of the white Boeing 767 as the landing gear hummed to life. He eyed endless green fields, a sparkling expanse of water, and a sprawling city along a river. The 44-year-old Cuban, who’d lost months of his life inside the vast network of U.S. immigration jails, was staring at his new purgatory: southern Ecuador.

His mind wasn’t on the reality of being stranded in this strange place; that despair would swallow him later. Instead, his thoughts were fixed on the piles of documents that had been taken by prison guards and vanished.

And now, he thought, I disappear too.

His deportee companions, mostly returning Ecuadorians and men from neighboring Peru, talked themselves into a frenzy over how they’d show journalists on the ground the deep and dark impressions on their wrists — evidence that they’d been tightly bound for more than 24 hours in hot and mostly stationary buses and planes with little water and infuriating discomfort. But when the plane landed at Aeropuerto Internacional José Joaquín de Olmedo minutes before noon on June 1, the tarmac was empty. Bolufé heard one man ask: “Don’t people worry about us?”

He was still wearing his dark green prison clothes when he stepped into the scorching midday sun, down the stairs and onto the runway. An American man in uniform handed him a sheet of paper.

“Pasaporte de emergencia,” it read. “Ecuatoriano nacido en Ecuador.”

Bolufé shot the man a confused look. The document was a blatant lie. Bolufé was not an “Ecuadorian born in Ecuador.” The Department of Homeland Security knew that. It was in his case file and detention records and plastered all over the internet thanks to his minor celebrity status in political circles back in Miami’s Little Havana.

But it had been days since he’d slept. And Bolufé had just ended an 11-day hunger strike over worsening detention conditions back in the United States, a protest he suspected had landed him this one-way trip to one of the most notorious cities in South America. In a split second, Bolufé decided he would not object. There was no way he’d wait for this to sort itself out while trapped at a local jail cell in the narco cartel city of Guayaquil. That would be a death sentence.

He handed the paper to an Ecuadorian immigration officer (who kept it), nodded when asked to verify the details, and was soon handed a blue drawstring bag from the Red Cross. Bolufé made his way to the airport’s passenger waiting area and sat on a black chair in the shadow of a silvery escalator. He pulled a bottle of milk from the bag and downed it in seconds.
881ECC2D-8D27-4FB9-B15D-DC77331F5088_1_201_a copy.jpg (4032x2268, AR: 1.78)For the next half hour, he considered his options. The U.S. government had ditched him in a foreign country with no money, no cellphone and no passport. His drab prison uniform, disheveled hair, and two-month scraggly beard made him unapproachable. His only identification was a green prison wristband and a CoreCivic commissary card — not official and, if anything, red flags.

Rogelio Enrique Bolufé Izquierdo — a Cuban man who had made his way through the archipelago of U.S. immigration detention centers, surviving the swampy dangers of Alligator Alcatraz in Florida and the frigid cells of an El Paso jail in Texas and the spreading diseases at Camp East Montana — was stuck.

* * *

Few Americans think of Ecuador, but when they do it’s usually in transit to the country’s national treasure: the Galápagos Islands. Lesser known is Guayaquil, a bustling port city that was once the global gateway for chocolate beans — historians recall how the thick and sweet aroma of drying cacao once hung over the entire town a century ago. Now, it’s probably where your bananas come from.

Guayaquil is situated 50 miles up the Guayas River from the Pacific Ocean, which makes it a key stop for cocaine cartels in nearby Colombia and Peru, and so the city has recently been overrun by crime.

In January 2024, the city briefly captured attention when more than a dozen gangsters with shotguns, submachine guns and sticks of dynamite took over a live broadcast of a local TV news station. By then, the nation that once boasted the lowest crime level in the region had become the most dangerous in the southern half of the globe. Guayaquil and the city of Durán, just across the river, have a combined homicide rate of roughly 90 per 100,000 — significantly higher than the District of Columbia’s darkest days in the 1990s. Even Guayaquil’s mayor, Aquiles Álvarez, has been arrested on corruption charges — and recently swore he’d keep leading from behind bars. (Last week, he received a three-year prison sentence.)

Even the airport isn’t safe. In mid-June, the leader of a gang called Los Águilas had just left the airport when two teens holding flower bouquets walked up and shot him dead.

But that only hints at the deteriorating situation on the ground, where thugs demand vacunas — which literally translates to “vaccines” but refers to the tolls paid to cross gang-controlled streets, a foreign concept for Ecuadorians that only appeared with the recent arrival of Tren de Aragua gangsters from Venezuela.
Ecuador Security (7700x4331, AR: 1.78)Ecuador Pineida Killed (5462x3073, AR: 1.78)Politically, Ecuador has become an echo of the United States. President Daniel Noboa has drawn public ridicule over his obsession with President Donald Trump: Both are rich guys who own a ton of shiny real estate and ran on promises of returning their countries to greatness.

Ecuador is also undergoing a nativist phase, blaming its problems on Venezuelan migrants. Bolufé and others deported there face a government that accepted them to acquiesce to a United States whose power looms large: Ecuador essentially has no control over its monetary policy, having ditched its currency 26 years ago and adopted the U.S. dollar.

Under Noboa, a U.S. citizen born in Miami, the country has become something of a client state — willing to accept scores of deportees like Bolufé but also giving American security forces broad license in the jungle. In June, he signed a decree granting U.S. troops immunity from criminal charges when going to war with alleged drug traffickers. The move came just months after a joint operation blew up a compound that locals professed was actually a dairy farm.

The U.S. government has designated the rival gangs Los Choneros and Los Lobos as foreign terrorist organizations. And the State Department has warned Americans not to travel north or south of a street that splits Guayaquil in half due to terrorism and crime — essentially making the entire city a no-go zone.

That profile makes it a curious deportation destination, as it’s become for more than 1,800 Cubans since the start of the second Trump administration. The strategy is a consequence of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller’s mission to rid the U.S. of undocumented people as quickly as possible, even through “third-country removals.” The July 2025 agreement between the United States and Ecuador pledges to seek a “dignified, safe, and timely transfer.” In reality, deportees’ final stop is a perilous place.

“It’s ‘plata o plomo,’” one former diplomat told me, echoing Pablo Escobar’s famous ultimatum: silver or lead.

“You either turn your eyes and get paid to look the other way or they kill you — and they start with your family,” the diplomat said. “It rivals the worst of conflicted places in Mexico.”

* * *

Bolufé knew he was in dire straits as soon as he walked out of the Guayaquil airport. He had no money, but he couldn’t receive a bank wire without identification. He couldn’t contact his ex-girlfriend via social media to send documents or money, because he couldn’t log in from a new and distant IP address without an incoming text to verify it was him. He couldn’t start a new online account without a phone number. And he couldn’t buy a phone.

He’d always been a hustler, having sold DirectTV and internet-connected computers growing up in communist Cuba. Now his old ways kicked in. He decided he’d offer a taxi driver money he didn't have. He strode past the Japanese koi pond and palm trees and made a straight shot for the back of the airport taxi line, betting that the last driver was most pressed for time. He played it cool and offered the man a hefty $20 an hour for a four-hour tour of the city.

They first stopped at the Sheraton and its pristine lobby decked out with modern art, where a concierge took one look at Bolufé’s prison uniform and informed him no rooms were available. Bolufé continued behind the lobby to look up other hotels on a public computer — but also to Google himself.

In the insular world of Cuban expatriate politics, Bolufé is a much-maligned enigma. Conservative blogs claim he was once a member of Fidel Castro’s personal security team and an agent for the Interior Ministry, which controls internal politics with secret police. Meanwhile, the Cuban government has branded him a terrorist and accused him of “fomenting, financing, and executing actions of sabotage” against the authoritarian regime there. Bolufé swears the truth is somewhere in between, saying he was part of a special class of insiders close to the Castro family who went by the name Departamento 0, an off-the-books task force authorized to eliminate bureaucracy by “zeroing out” bad policies — think DOGE, not assassinations.
Bolufe shakes hands with Fidel Castro in 2016 shortly before his death copy.jpg (1536x864, AR: 1.78)The next stop was the Marriott, where the lobby smelled like vanilla and a rack of Panama hats lined the left wall. By then, the taxi driver knew something was wrong. Bolufé had borrowed his phone to reach out to his ex-girlfriend, Haymel de la Vega, who promptly sent a picture of his Cuban passport while a cousin promised to wire funds. That image was enough to book a room, but the driver was still in the lurch. To calm him while the wire made its way south, Bolufé offered to buy a round of beers at the hotel bar — with money he didn’t yet have. They ordered Cerveza Club Premium and sat at a glossy wooden table for two in the corner, beneath a white geometric wall where the uplighting cast sharp shadows. Bolufé remembered discussing “banal, trivial things” for hours until the driver was alerted by phone that the wire had come through. They snuck out of the restaurant and left an open tab while they picked up the cash.

It was well past midnight by the time Bolufé managed to pay the driver, hotel and bar. He took the elevator to the Marriott’s top floor and sat by the pool, “just to appreciate the beauty of it.” He was still in his prison uniform. He hadn’t bathed in two days, and once again, he was penniless. He spent an hour on a lawn chair by the pool’s bright green astroturf deck, staring at the mirror-like water and imagining what it would feel like to jump in.

The next two weeks were a dizzying maze as Bolufé moved to cheaper and cheaper lodging to match the trickle of funds coming in from friends.

On Day 2, a faraway buddy used a shady online broker to order a smartphone that died hours after Bolufé picked it up. He ended up acquiring an “ENV,” a local brand that features a spartan helmet on the back. He grew wary as he took stock of the situation in the streets. Armed robbery is such an everyday affair that no sensible person wears a backpack on their back, and even old ladies wear them like stomach pouches. Private security guards in vests stand by the doors of coffee shops, grocers and the indigenous artisanal market downtown. And given that robbers nearly all ride motorcycles for a quick getaway, pedestrians on the sidewalk reflexively head further from the road when they rev by. It was no wonder the country’s president had decreed an “internal armed conflict” with nearly two dozen criminal groups labeled terrorists.

On Day 10, he managed to open an account at a local bank by bribing the teller with the bulk of the $120 a friend had sent. Transaction records on the app show he gets about $20 a day, usually from the same dedicated friend.

It wasn’t until Day 17 that another friend flew in from Miami — and was too nervous to leave the hotel. He dropped off a suitcase with Bolufé’s Cuban passport and a few clothes — black sweatpants and a Hawke & Co. jacket. Someone had heard it was winter south of the equator. Technically, yes, but in Ecuador that means 90-degree days and constant rain.

One of Bolufé’s half-dozen stops was a tiny Airbnb apartment that gave him the creeps. His suspicions turned out well-founded: One night, just before midnight, he was watching Netflix naked in bed when a man barged in, dressed all in black. Bolufé reached for a chef’s knife in the kitchen. “Well, that’s it, we’re ready to die,” he said, and pushed the man out. When he hurriedly texted the proprietor, he got the sense that the man was in on it. Nowhere seemed safe.

* * *

I first came across Bolufé while researching allegations of human rights violations at Alligator Alcatraz in the Florida Everglades.

How he got there was a tale unto its own. He had once run a club in Havana, but he got stuck on a trip to Miami during the COVID-19 closures. Without a work visa, he got by on eBay selling rare Cuban literature he found at an estate sale. He remade himself in Miami as someone who books reggaeton performers, and it was after a recording session on Aug. 17, 2025, that his crew got pulled over by Hialeah cops who wrote in their report that they found “a small clear plastic baggie with white powdery substance resembling cocaine” in his pocket when he stepped out of his client’s Lamborghini. Bolufé posted bail, but Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents grabbed him, hauling him to the new swamp detention camp that had become the butt of Trump’s jokes. “Don’t run in a straight line,” the president once said, making a zig-zag motion with his hands to advise on how to avoid getting eaten by alligators.

When Bolufé called the only number he could remember — the one belonging to his ex-girlfriend — she was bewildered.

“What are you talking about?” she said. “You don’t do drugs.”
Bolufe having coffee in Versailles, Miami's premiere hangout spot for Cuban expatriates copy.jpg (1199x1600, AR: 0.75)De la Vega, a health care consultant armed with ChatGPT and a dream of one day being a lawyer, helped him write habeas corpus lawsuits in 2025. She spent hours organizing documents, figuring out how to file them and talking to reporters. Bolufé lodged an asylum claim, arguing that the same Cuban government that branded him a terrorist would harm him. De la Vega’s aspirations wilted when her ex-boyfriend’s fellow inmates begged for her help too. By the time she connected me with him, she sounded exhausted.

In the months that followed, Bolufé became my connection within the ICE detention system.

He attested to how guards were punishing prisoners by forcing them into a small cage on the tarmac of the converted airport, exposed to the swamp’s blistering summer sun and relentless mosquitos. His eyes grew wide when he described what it felt like to be chained to an eyebolt on the floor, forced to wear a thin prison outfit while surrounded by guards in parkas as the air in the massive prison tent dropped to what felt like 40 degrees.

At one point, he sent me a petition signed by him and 39 fellow detainees from Brazil, Guatemala, Haiti and elsewhere that read “I was tortured in Alligator Alcatraz.” Bolufé’s accompanying statement said, “The lights stayed on 24 hours a day, and there were constant noises of chains hitting the floor, along with headcounts up to 20 times per day, making it impossible to sleep or rest.”
Documents I've received by mail from Bolufe for months copy.jpg (4646x2614, AR: 1.78)While at New Mexico’s Torrance County Detention Facility, he connected me to men who alleged mistreatment after witnessing guards suffocate to death Cuban detainee Geraldo Lunas Campos at Camp East Montana in Texas. And he flooded my P.O. box with letters and collected signatures from fellow detainees decrying the conditions behind bars at ICE facilities nationwide. He even helped organize La Union de Secuestrados por ICE, a kind of union of detainees “kidnapped by ICE.” Sketches by one inmate depict scenes from inside the compound: fungus growing on an Igloo water cooler and mold spreading from a crack in the wall to an air conditioning vent.

To pass the time, Bolufé read Nietzsche, The Alchemist, and Sun Tzu, gifts from friends on the outside. He started petitions, filed countless grievances, and went on something of a crusade demanding that the private prison contractor CoreCivic build a proper legal library at its New Mexico detention facility. Bolufé considered it absurdist humor when what eventually appeared was a tiny reading nook — with fiction books.

On May 7, guards snatched two boxes of his personal documents. Bolufé went on a hunger strike. ICE ping-ponged him across the country — a tactic he thought was an attempt to break him. Government records show he was transferred from the New Mexico jail to Camp East Montana, then to the overcrowded Arizona Removal Operations Coordination Center at Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport, then to the privately run Northwest ICE Processing Center in Washington, and finally to two other ICE locations in Arizona. The strangest leg of that tour was an 1,100-mile flight aboard an Embraer 145. Bolufé and a single other detainee were placed aboard the 50-seat private jet surrounded by guards — something he complained was a waste of American taxpayer funds. Gillian Brockell, an independent journalist who tracks ICE flights, pointed to government contracting price sheets that estimate the flight cost upwards of $25,000, not including fuel and insurance.

An immigration judge rejected Bolufé’s asylum claim. The stated reason for deportation was straightforward: Bolufé had overstayed his tourist visa that expired in July 2020. His journey through ICE detention came to an end when the Board of Immigration Appeals — which has been largely replaced by appointees aligned with MAGA’s maximalist deportation policies — wouldn’t reconsider the ruling.

Asked by NOTUS about the circumstances of his deportation and the inaccurate paperwork he received, DHS asserted that Bolufé has dual citizenship in Ecuador — something he immediately rejected. Bolufé said he briefly ran a bar in a Cuban neighborhood in northern Ecuador 15 years ago but returned to Cuba.

“I’m a Cuban citizen, born in Cuba on January 25, 1982 at 11:00 at night at the Línea maternity hospital,” he texted me. “I’m not an Ecuadorian citizen, nor do I have citizenship in any other country.”

As for Bolufé’s personal effects, DHS told NOTUS that “ICE ensures all of their personal property is controlled and safeguarded” but did not say what happened to his diary or other possessions. The department also said that “any claim that there are subprime conditions at ICE detention facilities is FALSE,” adding that “ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens.”

DHS did not answer questions about third-country removals to Ecuador or the safety concerns around transporting migrants to a place like Guayaquil. Instead, it offered a warning to other undocumented immigrants.

“Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now,” an unidentified spokesperson emailed NOTUS on Tuesday afternoon.

* * *

When Bolufé reached out to me in mid-June, he was at a cheap hotel in a terrible part of Guayaquil, calling from a number I didn’t recognize.

“I can’t even begin to explain how illegal this is,” he said in Spanish on the phone, his usual cheery tone replaced by one of utter exasperation. “I look homeless. It’s just inhumane, leaving someone with that degree of vulnerability in a country with this level of crime.”

A week later, I met him at the rundown Hotel Presidente Economy. The sagging porte-cochère faces a dilapidated street where men with hard stares stand by their off-road bikes and women spend their days building papier-mâché statues they hope to sell at Christmastime. The hotel entrance’s heavy metal doors are kept locked at all times, but the rooms have loose knobs that barely keep them shut. Windows face the corrugated tin roofs of the nearby buildings. Salsa and reggaeton blast late into the night, and the occasional gunshots barely register above the music and the street dogs that begin to howl around midnight. It’s a block north of Portete de Tarqui — that street the State Department uses to divide the scary part of town from the other scary part of town.

In Room 102, Bolufé’s clothes were piled in the corner near a pink suitcase — evidence of the thin lifeline he maintains to friends in Miami. The RCA air-conditioning unit on the wall struggled to keep up with the heat and squealed like a dying car engine. Bolufé sighed, wondering if he’d have to change rooms.

“All this moving around has me really uneasy,” he said. “I’ve had too many changes in the last few days.”

His most pressing concern was that Meta spam controls kept locking him out of his WhatsApp account for hours at a time. That tether of hope kept getting snipped.

“It’s every day, Monday to Monday,” he said, holding up his phone. “I’ve been here for 20 days, and in those 20 days, this happens every day, at all hours.”

Bolufé had $100.44 in the bank and was sporting the unmistakable thin strap of a cheap, black Casio F-91W watch. His nails were long, but his hair was short. The unkempt beard was now trimmed into a goatee of sorts. He moved slowly and shook as he spoke, chain-smoking Camel Blues while sipping the free coffee from the lobby. The machine would break the next day, but at that moment the brew was hot.

We found chairs surrounded by stone walls in a back alcove. The Ecuador-Germany World Cup game played on a TV nearby. When Ecuador scored its winning goal, car horns blared on Ambato Avenue. Cheers erupted in the streets. Bolufé took a long drag from his cigarette.

“My life has been an accident,” he said.
70C0F748-DFB4-484E-B354-8C148378A1B8_1_201_a copy.jpg (4032x2268, AR: 1.78)Bolufe meets Roger Stone at a gun show in West Palm Beach copy.jpg (1496x841, AR: 1.78)He would have been busy at that moment if those jail guards hadn’t taken his personal diary. Bolufé had dreamed of leaving ICE detention — how exactly was always a hazy idea — and writing a memoir he hoped would one day echo the tales of Soviet dissident Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn in The Gulag Archipelago.

“I’m not a materialist person,” he said. “But when they took away my papers, that actually hurt. How are you going to take away the pitiful little proof I have against you? How can you fight for your rights against the very power that’s imprisoning you? They have all the best lawyers, and all that money, and here I am with my little papers.”

The conversation shifted to his past life in Cuba. Behind audacious sunglasses I keep asking him to take off, Bolufé swore he knew everybody: Fidel Castro’s adult kids — even secret ones — who fell under his watch, musical artists he discovered on the street, influential government officials. He kept insisting he was a self-made man with all the right connections. But where were they now?

Bolufé stared at his phone while scrolling WhatsApp. If they didn’t check in on him now, he said, they probably never really cared.

His primary concern was how to get by each day, which was difficult enough in a place where some coffee shops and taxis request an Ecuadorian government ID number just to hand over a receipt. But the gnawing concern in the background was figuring out how to get out of the country. The way he landed there, he feared, could make escape harder.

“I have the stigma of being deported here,” he told me, “and having been deported here is already a very bad mark against you when applying for a visa to any other country.”

Over the next few days, Bolufé mostly stayed holed up inside the hotel, too proud to say he was afraid to venture out but forthcoming enough to admit he wanted nothing to do with the battered streets of the city’s Ayacucho district. He’d become a regular at the Capitán Barbosa because it was right around the corner and the flamboyant restaurateur Ricki let him rack up a tab. One evening, an old man with a belly as round as his plate’s mound of white rice motioned for Bolufé to swing by. The viejito whispered a warning: A woman was robbed at gunpoint at our table the night before. We sat down, and my companion pulled out his ENV phone to show me something. The old man grunted and shook his head. Don’t pull it out, idiot.

One morning, I ventured to a corner bakery on the street mentioned in the State Department advisory. Battered police pickups sped by every few minutes. Rival gangs fight over these city blocks, also claimed by a little black mutt who marked his territory on the northeast corner of Portete de Tarqui and Seis de Marzo. When it was time to pay for a beef empanada, I reached into my pocket and found it empty. I glanced back just in time to see my missing $5 bill in the thick fingers of a stout man, rubbing it to examine his discovery. He glanced at the sky, and made the sign of the cross. I let him keep it.

Later, I persuaded Bolufé to guide me around the city so I could retrace his steps, first at the airport then at various hotels. During lunch at one point, he stressed the need to start planting roots at this new place he refused to call home.

“I need to socialize and make some connections," he said. “In reality, I’m quite alone here.”

It was a Friday, and Bolufé decided he’d start at the most unlikely of places in this typically Catholic city, where nuns can be seen picking up a salty pan de ambato at pastry shops. Bolufé claims to have converted to Islam sometime during his 286-day ICE detention, having discovered the benefits of that tight-knit community behind bars. So we visited the Centro Islámico Guayaquil for its Salah al-Jum'ah midday service. The imam, speaking in Spanish but singing recitations in Arabic, said exactly what Bolufé needed to hear: The misfortunes one endures are nothing — all that matters are the teachings of Allah.

“Islam does not depend on the life and death of others,” the imam repeated.
F7716336-DA42-4DF8-9C97-B482D8241FD0_1_201_a copy.jpg (4032x2268, AR: 1.78)Afterward, three dozen men set up a table and distributed free styrofoam containers of rice, potato salad and shredded beef.

“Óyeme, this food is great,” Bolufé chimed in, hoping to spark conversation with potential new friends. “Who’s the chef?”

“The sisters cooked it,” responded a baby-faced man to our right.

“One would hope one of the sisters is single,” said another to our left, drawing chuckles all around.

Bolufé began to work the room, settling in on a beefy guy in a skullcap who carried himself like a man who’d done time. After a brief chat, Bolufé raced back.

“He’s a Cuban from Miami!” he whispered.

“Also deported?” I asked.

“He doesn’t want to tell me yet.”

* * *

In another part of town, inside a tall tower and behind four locked doors, is a local non-governmental organization called the Committee for the Defense of Human Rights. Its president, Billy Navarette, listened intently as I described Bolufé’s situation. The organization is concerned about what it means to have so many foreigners dumped into a city that’s become a battleground for drug cartels that could prey on desperate migrants.

“Inevitably, they’ll need to talk to these gangsters,” he said. “It’s a reality. They have control.”

He assessed Bolufé’s situation. A Cuban passport wouldn’t get Bolufé far, because it bore no stamp of him having entered the country — thanks to the inaccurate paperwork Bolufé was handed on his way in.

“It’s something extraordinary,” Navarette said.
47050875-FB65-429B-B2E5-52FCA6024ECC_1_201_a copy.jpg (4032x2268, AR: 1.78)Navarette thought about what to do. With some work — and some pleading with Ecuadorian officials — CDH might be able to get Bolufé’s documents in order so he can legally be present in Ecuador. Until then, it’s dangerous for him to go anywhere without an ID. Bolufé is once again an undocumented immigrant. I told Navarette how Bolufé, in a fit of inspiration, had concocted an idea to put together a reggaeton event in neighboring Peru later in the summer. Navarette winced.

“His asylum application in the United States could prove useful here,” he said. “But it’s a long process. It takes years.”

Part of the challenge is political. Maria Teresa Urueña, a program manager with the nonpartisan Center for Engagement and Advocacy in the Americas, told me that Bolufé faces an Ecuador that is less tolerant of people like him — regardless of the diplomatic deals that make these third-country removals possible.

“The deportation machine has become more sophisticated … and what protection can Ecuador really provide these asylees? Ecuador is not a safe place,” she said, noting that even she canceled a trip to Guayaquil in April due to security concerns.

Mobile Pathways, a tech nonprofit that monitors third-country expulsions and tracks court data, counted 1,836 Cubans who have been deported to Ecuador since the start of the second Trump administration. According to the Ecuadorian government, 94 of them have arrived in Ecuador seeking asylum in 2026 so far.

But there’s a flood on the horizon. According to Third Country Deportation Watch, a joint project between two humanitarian organizations, the U.S. immigration system in just the six months between December and June has put 18,552 people who aren’t from Ecuador on track for a forced deportation there. Among them are thousands of Venezuelans, Cubans, Guatemalans — and even a few from Burkina Faso, a West African nation that has become a battleground for Islamist militias.

Those who track U.S. deportation flights say they now arrive at Guayaquil airport three times a week on Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays.

* * *

During my layover in Miami on the way to Ecuador, I was reminded of the alternate reality on display in conservative Little Havana. The old Cuban-American guard hanging out at outdoor coffee shops still have MAGA bumper stickers on their pickup trucks. The fear of mistreatment and expulsion is only real for recent newcomers like Jose Reina, who fled Cuba and trekked across most of Central America with the help of a $5,000 human trafficking coyote. He managed to get legal status at the tail end of the Biden administration and now works at a hotel in South Florida.

“Those people that defend Trump are blind — no different than the communists I knew on the island," he said. “One has to think for themselves.”

That’s not a parallel you hear often in Cuban-American circles, where politics have been dominated by Republican Party identity for decades. But it’s different for those at the receiving end of the Trump administration’s deportation apparatus.

Sitting on a lawn chair on a hill overlooking the dark waters of the Guayas River, Bolufé admitted that he admired Trump’s nostalgic vision of America and cheered him on — until he saw what ICE agents and private contractor prison guards were willing to do to detainees like him.

“You might think I’m crazy, and maybe I am. But I learned a lot being stuck in those ICE prisons, watching people suffering mental problems — the way due process and the Constitution is violated, the way people violate basic human rights, the way DHS and ICE lie unscrupulously,” he said.

Then he offered up something unexpected: Despite the chains and cold rooms and moldy shower stalls, he would have preferred to remain in ICE detention than get sent to Ecuador. At least it was a labyrinth he had learned to navigate.
6BE36A02-F2D3-432B-9B83-C0743911833E_1_201_a copy.jpg (4032x2268, AR: 1.78)That traumatic past was starting to fade into the background. All the jail transfers and quarrels with guards were blurring together, Bolufé said, and he’d rather look forward than wrestle memories. My days with him in Guayaquil had jolted his inner drive, long suppressed from “everything that happened." He pulled up his phone and tapped the screen. He began recording a voice note asking a reggaeton agent if his client would be interested in booking a show. When his cigarettes ran out, he treated himself to my pack and pulled out another. He turned his back to the river and called a buddy in Miami who asked what he was doing next.

He had big plans. He was headed to Mexico, he said — although he was unsure how he’d travel there. Or maybe Spain, where he’d claim some sort of asylum. Or maybe Egypt, to embrace his new faith, although he didn’t know a lick of Arabic. Well, he knew one word.

“Inshallah,” he said, with a wave of his left hand.
entries.author: Jose Pagliery

entries.title: The Democratic Establishment Strikes Back in Wisconsin
entries.summary: In a shocker, David Crowley beat democratic socialist Francesca Hong for the Democratic nomination in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race.
entries.content:
David Crowley’s campaign rose from the dead and saved the Democratic establishment in Wisconsin — defeating democratic socialist Francesca Hong for the Democratic nomination in the state’s gubernatorial race.

In a dramatic, nail-biting finish, Crowley pulled off a massive upset in the swing state, where he mounted a three-week comeback to overtake Hong, whose leftist and politically fringe comments haunted her closing sprint. Crowley, who exited the multicandidate primary in early July and jumped back in a week later, was propelled by an endorsement from Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Crowley will now face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in November.

“Now, David is focused on bringing people together, earning the support of Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and anyone who believes Wisconsin is at its best when we work together and deliver results,” said Garren Randolph, Crowley’s campaign manager, in a statement.

The Associated Press called the race for Crowley shortly after 3:30 a.m. ET on Wednesday.

“I think primary voters freaked out about her electability, saying and doing weird stuff, and late deciders broke for him,” said Adam Carlson, a Democratic pollster. “Anxious voters who don’t want Tom Tiffany, an election-denier, and Wisconsin voters are well-trained, perennial swing state voters. Stakes are too high.”

Crowley’s victory cuts against recent progressive gains in New York City, Denver and Michigan — and raises serious questions over primary polling ahead of the 2028 presidential primary.

“The Democratic Party is going to have to grapple with how broken primary polls are ahead of 2028,” said Amanda Litman, co-founder of the progressive Run For Something, which endorsed Hong in her state legislative races. “Historically they’ve been part of the calculation for things like debate thresholds — that no longer makes sense, if it ever did.”

In Wisconsin, Crowley styled himself as the more electable candidate compared to Hong, whose leftist views and woke-era social media posts made Democrats in the state uneasy about her chances of beating Tiffany in November. The Republican Governors Association dropped more than $3 million on ads boosting Hong, an effort Crowley frequently highlighted on the campaign trail as evidence that Hong was the weaker general election candidate.

Hong led the polls in the final weeks of what had been a chaotic and crowded primary. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, exited the race in early July because his campaign wasn’t gaining traction. He reentered with Evers’ support after Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out following reporting inaccuracies in her campaign finance reports. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, another candidate, dropped out soon after, shortly before the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported that it was looking into allegations of sexual impropriety.

A private August 5 memo, circulated by the Crowley campaign and obtained by NOTUS, argued that the primary electorate would ultimately mirror a traditional Wisconsin primary electorate and be “far older than the electorate being polled.” That path for Crowley ultimately bore out on Tuesday, along with a surge of late-deciders who ultimately sided with Crowley, several Wisconsin Democrats said.

"I am so proud of David—he's the future of our Party, and I can't wait for him to be our next governor," Evers said in a social media post. "For now, we polka. Tomorrow, we're back at work to win."

The large group of voters who were undecided late in the campaign appeared to break for Crowley, showing his stronger name ID and get-out-the-vote operation, said Brandon Scholz, an independent strategist in Wisconsin.

“Everybody chose to ignore the 20 percent undecided voters,” said a Wisconsin Democratic strategist, granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly. “We never saw a youth surge that was reshaping the electorate."

Late Tuesday night, before the race was decided, Hong told her supporters that “in 11 weeks, no matter who is on this ballot y’all, we are going to fight to win together.”

Hong’s loss does come with vindication for at least some progressives. National progressive stars who had rushed into other Democratic primaries sat out the Wisconsin race. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) didn’t endorse Hong, staying conspicuously absent from the primary just a week after helping push Abdul El-Sayed over the line in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary.

Skepticism of primary polls grew last week after El-Sayed only narrowly beat Rep. Haley Stevens, despite polls for weeks showing him up substantially.

Crowley now faces a potentially challenging contest against Tiffany in a battleground state that President Donald Trump narrowly won in 2024. But Tiffany will have to reckon with Trump’s unpopularity and his own denial of the 2020 election results.

Wisconsin Republicans are left privately grappling with the reality they didn’t get their preferred candidate. One Wisconsin Republican operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly, acknowledged that “the entire Republican playbook was based on the certainty of running against a Socialist deeply out of touch with any corner of Wisconsin that isn’t Dane County.”

“Whoops,” they added.

—
Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.
